subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between RAM and ROM.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile; RAM can be read from and written to, ROM is (normally) read-only.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: RAM volatile / ROM non-volatile; RAM read and write / ROM read only; RAM stores data and programs currently in use / ROM stores the start-up instructions (bootstrap/BIOS); RAM contents change while the computer runs / ROM contents are fixed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A washing machine sold in Lahore stores its wash programs in ROM. Explain why ROM is used for this.
parts.answer: The wash programs must not be lost when the machine is switched off, and they must not be changed by the user.
parts.working: 1 mark: ROM is non-volatile so the programs are kept when power is off. 1 mark: ROM cannot be written to/changed so the programs cannot be accidentally altered or deleted.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha stores her photographs on a solid-state drive (SSD) in her laptop. Identify whether an SSD is primary or secondary storage.
parts.answer: Secondary storage.
parts.working: B1 secondary (non-volatile, not directly accessed by the CPU).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three reasons why an SSD is more suitable than a magnetic hard disk drive for a laptop that is carried to school every day.
parts.answer: No moving parts so more robust/less likely to be damaged if dropped; lighter and thinner; uses less power so the battery lasts longer (also faster access, silent).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no moving parts / more durable if knocked; lighter; smaller/thinner; lower power consumption so longer battery life; faster read/write access; runs cooler; silent.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is stored on a magnetic hard disk drive.
parts.answer: Platters coated in magnetic material spin; a read/write head moves across the surface on an actuator arm; it magnetises tiny areas in one of two directions to represent 1 and 0; data is stored in tracks and sectors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: uses (rotating) platters; surface coated with a magnetisable material; read/write head on an actuator arm moves across the platter; tiny areas (domains) are magnetised; magnetised in one of two directions to represent 1 or 0; platter divided into tracks and sectors; head reads by detecting the direction of magnetisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A video-editing studio in Karachi keeps 40 TB of archived footage. Explain why magnetic storage is still often chosen for this instead of solid-state storage.
parts.answer: Magnetic storage has a lower cost per gigabyte and is available in very large capacities, and the archive does not need very fast access.
parts.working: 1 mark: cheaper per unit of storage / large capacity at low cost. 1 mark: speed of access is less important for archive data / data is accessed rarely.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by virtual memory.
parts.answer: Part of secondary storage (e.g. the hard disk or SSD) is used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full.
parts.working: 1 mark: an area of secondary storage is used as (an extension of) RAM. 1 mark: used when RAM is full / to hold pages of data or programs not currently needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how virtual memory is used when a student opens many large applications at once.
parts.answer: When RAM becomes full, data/pages that are not currently being used are moved from RAM to virtual memory on secondary storage, freeing RAM for the data needed now; when those pages are needed again they are swapped back into RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: RAM fills up; pages/data not currently in use are transferred to virtual memory (secondary storage); space in RAM is then used for the new data/application; pages are swapped back into RAM when needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one drawback of relying heavily on virtual memory.
parts.answer: It is much slower than RAM, so the computer slows down (disk thrashing).
parts.working: B1 slower access than RAM / disk thrashing / extra wear on an SSD.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define cloud storage.
parts.answer: Storing data on remote servers (owned by a third party) that are accessed over the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark: data stored on (remote/off-site) servers. 1 mark: accessed using the internet / managed by a third-party company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A football club in Manchester is deciding whether to keep its match videos on cloud storage or on its own local server. Give two benefits and two drawbacks of using cloud storage.
parts.answer: Benefits: can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection; provider handles backups/maintenance; storage can be increased easily; no need to buy hardware. Drawbacks: needs an internet connection; monthly fees; security depends on a third party; data could be lost if the provider fails; uploads/downloads may be slow.
parts.working: 2 marks for benefits, any two of: access from any location/device with internet; easy to share files; provider backs up data and maintains hardware; scalable; no hardware purchase or maintenance cost. 2 marks for drawbacks, any two of: requires internet access; ongoing subscription cost; data security/privacy controlled by third party; risk of provider outage or closure; slow transfer of large files.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a solid-state drive stores data.
parts.answer: It uses flash memory made of transistors (NAND/NOR); electric charge is trapped in a floating gate (control gate and floating gate) to represent a 1 or 0; there are no moving parts, and the charge stays when power is removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: uses flash memory / semiconductor chips; made of transistors; control gate and floating gate; electrons/charge trapped in the floating gate; presence or absence of charge represents 1 or 0; non-volatile – charge remains without power; no moving parts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how data is stored on an optical disc such as a DVD.
parts.answer: A laser burns/creates pits and lands on a spiral track on the disc surface; to read, a laser is shone on the track and the reflection differs between pits and lands, representing 1s and 0s.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: laser used to write and read; pits and lands; on a single spiral track; reflected light is detected; pits scatter light / lands reflect it; the difference represents binary 1 and 0.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hospital in Islamabad needs storage for three purposes. For each, name the most suitable type of storage (magnetic, optical, solid state or cloud) and justify your choice.
(i) The start-up instructions of a heart-rate monitor's control board.
(ii) A portable device carried by doctors on ward rounds to record notes.
(iii) Off-site copies of patient records so they survive a fire in the building.
parts.answer: (i) ROM / solid state (flash) in the device – non-volatile and must not be changed. (ii) Solid state – no moving parts so robust if dropped, small, low power. (iii) Cloud storage – stored off-site on remote servers, so it is not destroyed by a fire at the hospital, and can be accessed from anywhere.
parts.working: For each part: 1 mark for a suitable storage type, 1 mark for a matching justification. (i) ROM/flash: non-volatile, instructions fixed. (ii) Solid state: durable, light, low power, fast. (iii) Cloud (or magnetic tape/disk stored off-site): physically separate location, protected from local disaster; accept magnetic with off-site justification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The hospital's computers have 8 GiB of RAM. Explain why adding more RAM can make a computer run faster when many programs are open.
parts.answer: More data and programs can be held in RAM at once, so less virtual memory (slow secondary storage) is needed and less time is spent swapping pages.
parts.working: 1 mark: more instructions/data can be stored in RAM. 1 mark: less need to use virtual memory / fewer slow transfers to and from secondary storage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a computer needs both primary storage and secondary storage.
parts.answer: Primary storage (RAM) is directly accessible by the CPU and fast, so it holds the data and instructions currently being used, but RAM is volatile and relatively expensive. Secondary storage is non-volatile and has large capacity at lower cost, so it keeps files and programs permanently when the power is off.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: primary storage is directly accessed by the CPU; RAM holds data/programs currently in use and is fast; RAM is volatile so contents lost when power off; secondary storage is non-volatile/permanent; secondary storage offers large capacity at lower cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says: 'If my laptop had 2 TB of RAM I would not need an SSD at all.' Give two reasons why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile, so all files and the operating system would be lost when the laptop is switched off; RAM is far more expensive per byte, so 2 TB would be extremely costly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: RAM is volatile – data lost when power off; nothing to load the OS from on start-up; RAM cost per GB much higher; ROM only holds the bootstrap so files still need permanent storage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the arithmetic logic unit (ALU).
parts.answer: It carries out calculations and logical operations (comparisons).
parts.working: B1 performs arithmetic (e.g. addition) and logic operations (e.g. AND, comparisons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the control unit (CU).
parts.answer: It sends control signals to manage the movement of data and instructions around the CPU, and decodes instructions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: sends control signals; controls the flow of data within the CPU and between the CPU and memory; decodes instructions; manages the fetch-decode-execute cycle / synchronises using the clock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
parts.answer: Program counter (PC).
parts.working: B1 program counter.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table lists four statements about registers and buses. For each statement, name the register or bus it describes.
1. Holds the data or instruction that has just been fetched from memory or is about to be written to memory.
2. Carries signals such as 'memory read' and 'memory write'.
3. Holds the address of the memory location that is about to be accessed.
4. Holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
parts.answer: 1 Memory data register (MDR); 2 Control bus; 3 Memory address register (MAR); 4 Current instruction register (CIR).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct name: MDR; control bus; MAR; CIR.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Refer to the registers and buses used.
parts.answer: The address in the PC is copied into the MAR; the address is sent along the address bus to memory; a read signal is sent on the control bus; the instruction at that address is sent along the data bus to the MDR; the instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR; the PC is incremented by 1.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: PC holds address of next instruction; address copied from PC to MAR; address sent via address bus; control unit sends read signal on control bus; instruction transferred via data bus; instruction stored in MDR; instruction copied to CIR; PC incremented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens in the decode stage.
parts.answer: The control unit decodes (interprets) the instruction in the CIR.
parts.working: B1 instruction in the CIR is decoded/interpreted by the control unit.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional but the data bus is bidirectional.
parts.answer: Addresses only travel from the CPU to memory, whereas data must travel both from memory to the CPU (reading) and from the CPU to memory (writing).
parts.working: 1 mark: address bus carries addresses only from CPU (MAR) to memory. 1 mark: data bus carries data to and from the CPU (read and write).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the accumulator (ACC).
parts.answer: It temporarily stores the result of calculations carried out by the ALU.
parts.working: B1 holds intermediate/final results of ALU operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During one cycle the PC contains 52. State the value in the PC after the fetch stage has finished, assuming instructions are stored one per address and no jump occurs.
parts.working: B1 53 – the PC is incremented by 1 during the fetch stage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An instruction is stored at memory address 200 and the next instruction is at address 201. The instruction at 200 tells the CPU to add the value stored at address 350 to the accumulator.
Describe, step by step, how the CPU fetches and executes this instruction, naming each register and bus involved.
parts.answer: Fetch: 200 is copied from PC to MAR; sent on address bus with a read signal on the control bus; instruction travels on data bus to MDR; copied to CIR; PC becomes 201. Decode: CU decodes the instruction in CIR. Execute: 350 is placed in the MAR; value at address 350 is read via the data bus into the MDR; the ALU adds the MDR value to the ACC; result is stored in the ACC.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: PC (200) → MAR; address bus used; read signal via control bus; instruction to MDR via data bus; MDR → CIR; PC incremented to 201; CU decodes instruction; operand address 350 → MAR; data at 350 loaded into MDR; ALU performs addition; result stored in ACC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the PC is incremented during the fetch stage instead of after the instruction has been executed.
parts.answer: So that it already holds the address of the next instruction, ready for the next cycle; if the instruction is a jump, the execute stage can then overwrite the PC with the new address.
parts.working: 1 mark: PC then points to the next instruction ready for the next fetch. 1 mark: a jump/branch instruction can replace the PC value during execute.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many computers are based on the Von Neumann model, in which instructions and data are stored in the same memory. Name the three buses that connect the CPU to memory.
parts.answer: Address bus, data bus and control bus.
parts.working: 1 mark each: address bus; data bus; control bus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by an instruction set.
parts.answer: The list of all the commands (machine code operations) that a particular CPU can process.
parts.working: 1 mark: a list/set of all the commands/operations. 1 mark: that the CPU can process / are built into the CPU (e.g. add, load, store, jump).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher describes the cycle as: 'The CU fetches an instruction, the ALU decodes it, and then it is executed.' Identify the error in the teacher's description and correct it.
parts.answer: The ALU does not decode instructions; the control unit decodes the instruction (the ALU only carries out arithmetic and logic during execute).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies that the ALU does not decode. 1 mark: correction – the CU decodes the instruction; ALU used only during execution of arithmetic/logic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the system clock in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
parts.answer: The clock sends out regular pulses that synchronise all CPU operations; each step of the cycle happens in time with the clock pulses.
parts.working: 1 mark: produces timing signals/pulses at a fixed rate. 1 mark: synchronises the components so each step of the FDE cycle occurs on a pulse.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what is held in the MAR and the MDR at the moment an instruction is being read from address 75, if the instruction stored there is 10110011.
parts.answer: MAR holds the address 75; MDR receives/holds the instruction 10110011.
parts.working: 1 mark: MAR = 75 (address). 1 mark: MDR = 10110011 (contents of that address).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Input and output devices

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify whether each device is an input device or an output device: barcode scanner, actuator, microphone, 3D printer, digital camera, LCD projector.
parts.answer: Input: barcode scanner, microphone, digital camera. Output: actuator, 3D printer, LCD projector.
parts.working: 1 mark for every two correct (6 correct = 3 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A supermarket in Peshawar uses barcode scanners at its tills. Give two benefits to the supermarket of using barcode scanners instead of typing product codes.
parts.answer: Faster checkout; fewer errors in entering codes; stock can be updated automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: faster data entry; more accurate than typing; automatic stock control/reordering; prices can be changed centrally; fewer staff needed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Input and output devices

parts.label: a
parts.text: A museum in Cairo wants to create exact copies of small ancient statues so visitors can handle them. Identify the two devices that would be needed and state the role of each.
parts.answer: A 3D scanner to capture the shape of the statue as a digital 3D model; a 3D printer to build the copy layer by layer from that model.
parts.working: 1 mark each: 3D scanner; captures the dimensions/shape to produce a digital (CAD) model; 3D printer; builds the physical copy in layers (additive manufacturing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between an inkjet printer and a laser printer.
parts.answer: Inkjet uses liquid ink sprayed through nozzles, laser uses powdered toner and a charged drum; laser is faster and better for high-volume printing, inkjet is cheaper to buy and better for small numbers of photo-quality prints.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: liquid ink vs powder toner; nozzles/droplets vs drum/static charge and fuser; laser faster for large volumes; inkjet cheaper to buy; laser cheaper per page in large volumes; inkjet better for small photo prints.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Input and output devices

parts.label: a
parts.text: A café in Lahore puts a QR code on each table. Customers scan it with their phone to open the menu. Give two advantages of a QR code compared with a traditional barcode.
parts.answer: A QR code can store much more data (e.g. a full URL); it can be read from any angle; it still works if partly damaged (built-in error correction); it can be read by a phone camera.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: stores more data; can hold a URL/text; readable from any direction; error correction allows reading if damaged; scanned with smartphone camera.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using QR codes in this way.
parts.answer: Customers need a smartphone with a camera and internet access; a fake QR code could link to a malicious website.
parts.working: B1 needs a smartphone/data; risk of malicious QR codes replacing genuine ones; difficult for some older customers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The café also uses an LED screen to show the order queue. State one reason an LED screen is more suitable than a projector for this.
parts.answer: It is bright enough to be seen clearly in a well-lit room (and needs no screen/space to project).
parts.working: B1 visible in bright light / no projection space needed / longer life / lower running cost.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Input and output devices

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory uses a robot arm controlled by a computer. Explain the role of an actuator in this system.
parts.answer: The actuator is an output device that receives a signal from the computer and turns it into physical movement, such as operating a motor to move the arm.
parts.working: 1 mark: output device controlled by electrical signals from the computer/microprocessor. 1 mark: produces physical movement (motor, valve, pump) e.g. moves or grips with the arm.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Recommend, with reasons, an input device and an output device for each situation.
(i) A visually impaired student who wants to use a computer to write essays.
(ii) A news reporter who needs to send pictures of a flood quickly to the newsroom.
parts.answer: (i) Input: microphone with speech recognition – no need to see a keyboard; output: speakers/headphones – text can be read aloud. (ii) Input: digital camera (or smartphone camera) – captures images digitally so they can be sent at once; output: monitor/screen to check the images before sending (or the newsroom's screen).
parts.working: Each part: 1 mark for a suitable input device with reason, 1 mark for a suitable output device with reason. Accept sensible alternatives such as a braille embosser for (i).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Input and output devices

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school hall has a DLP projector. State one input device and one output device that a teacher would use to present a lesson in the hall.
parts.answer: Input: keyboard/mouse (or microphone); output: projector (or speakers).
parts.working: 1 mark for a suitable input device; 1 mark for a suitable output device.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The hall also has loudspeakers. Describe how a loudspeaker turns the digital sound data from the computer into sound.
parts.answer: The digital data is converted to an analogue signal by a DAC and amplified; the varying current flows through a coil, creating a changing magnetic field that interacts with a permanent magnet, so the coil and attached cone vibrate; the vibrations produce sound waves in the air.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: DAC converts digital data to an analogue signal; signal is amplified; varying current in a coil produces a changing magnetic field; interaction with a permanent magnet makes the coil/cone move back and forth (vibrate); vibrating cone creates sound waves.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU performance, cores, cache and embedded systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three factors that affect the performance of a CPU.
parts.answer: Clock speed, number of cores, size of cache.
parts.working: 1 mark each: clock speed; number of cores; cache size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A CPU has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz. State how many clock cycles it performs each second.
parts.answer: 3 200 000 000 (3.2 billion) cycles per second.
parts.working: B1 3.2 × 10⁹ cycles per second.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU performance, cores, cache and embedded systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how increasing the size of the cache can improve the performance of a CPU.
parts.answer: Cache is very fast memory close to (inside) the CPU; it stores frequently used instructions and data; a larger cache can hold more of them, so the CPU has to fetch from slower RAM less often.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: cache is faster than RAM; stores frequently used data/instructions; larger cache holds more, so fewer slower RAM accesses / instructions fetched faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hassan says that a quad-core processor will always run his programs four times faster than a single-core processor of the same clock speed. Explain why he is wrong.
parts.answer: Not all programs can be split into tasks that run in parallel; the cores also have to communicate with each other, which takes time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: software may not be written to use multiple cores; some tasks must be done in sequence; time is lost communicating between cores; shared resources/bus limit speed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU performance, cores, cache and embedded systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term embedded system.
parts.answer: A combination of hardware and software built into a larger device to perform one dedicated function.
parts.working: 1 mark: microprocessor-based system (hardware and software) built into a device. 1 mark: performs a specific/dedicated task.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which two of the following contain an embedded system: a smart air conditioner, a laptop used for homework, a car's anti-lock braking system, a desktop computer in a library.
parts.answer: Smart air conditioner; car's anti-lock braking system.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Laptops and desktops are general-purpose computers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two benefits of using embedded systems in household appliances.
parts.answer: Small and cheap to mass-produce; low power consumption; reliable; can be controlled remotely when connected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: small size; low cost; low power use; fast response; reliable/little maintenance; can be controlled remotely.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU performance, cores, cache and embedded systems

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A games company compares two CPUs:
CPU X: 4 cores, 2.8 GHz, 6 MB cache
CPU Y: 2 cores, 3.6 GHz, 3 MB cache
The company's game engine runs many tasks in parallel. Recommend one CPU for the company and justify your choice by referring to all three factors.
parts.answer: CPU X: although its clock speed is lower, it has twice as many cores so more parallel tasks can be processed at the same time, and its larger cache means more data/instructions are close to the CPU, reducing slow accesses to RAM; CPU Y's higher clock speed processes more instructions per second per core but this is less important for parallel workloads.
parts.working: 1 mark: recommends X. 1 mark: more cores allow tasks to run in parallel. 1 mark: larger cache, fewer accesses to RAM. 1 mark: acknowledges Y has higher clock speed/more cycles per second but this advantage is outweighed (accept a well-justified Y only if it uses all three factors, max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why doubling the clock speed of a CPU may not double the speed at which programs run.
parts.answer: Other parts of the system, such as RAM, buses and storage, may not keep up, so the CPU waits for data; higher speed also causes more heat, which may lead to the CPU slowing itself down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: bottleneck in memory/bus/storage speed; CPU waits for data; overheating causes throttling; program may be limited by input/output.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Sensors and microprocessor control

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the most suitable sensor for each of these uses:
(i) detecting when the water in a rooftop tank in Multan reaches the top
(ii) checking whether the soil in a greenhouse plant pot is dry
(iii) detecting smoke or carbon monoxide in a kitchen
(iv) detecting a car approaching a barrier at a car park
parts.answer: (i) level sensor; (ii) moisture sensor; (iii) gas sensor; (iv) proximity sensor (accept infrared or magnetic field sensor).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Sensors and microprocessor control

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A greenhouse in Murree uses a temperature sensor and a microprocessor to control a heater and a window motor. The temperature should stay between 18 °C and 26 °C.
Describe how the system keeps the temperature in this range.
parts.answer: The temperature sensor continually sends readings; they are converted from analogue to digital by an ADC; the microprocessor compares each reading with the stored values 18 and 26; if the reading is below 18 the microprocessor sends a signal to switch the heater on (and close the window); if the reading is above 26 it switches the heater off and sends a signal to the actuator/motor to open the window; if it is in range, heater off and window closed (no change); the process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: sensor sends readings to microprocessor; ADC converts analogue to digital; preset values stored; reading compared with 18 and 26; below 18 → heater on / window closed; above 26 → heater off, signal to actuator to open window; between → no action/heater off; the loop continues/readings taken at intervals.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Sensors and microprocessor control

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car has a parking-assist system that uses sensors and a microprocessor. When the car is closer than 50 cm to an object, a buzzer beeps.
Name a suitable sensor for this system.
parts.answer: Proximity sensor (accept ultrasonic/infrared distance sensor).
parts.working: B1 proximity sensor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the microprocessor uses data from the sensor to control the buzzer.
parts.answer: The sensor continuously sends data; the data is converted to digital; the microprocessor compares the distance with the stored value 50 cm; if it is less than 50 cm it sends a signal to switch the buzzer on, otherwise the buzzer is off; this repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: sensor sends readings; ADC converts to digital; compared with stored value (50 cm); less than 50 → signal to turn buzzer on; otherwise buzzer off; process repeats continuously.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one improvement so that the driver gets more information as the car gets closer.
parts.answer: The microprocessor makes the beeps faster (or louder) as the distance decreases.
parts.working: B1 frequency/rate of beeping increases as distance falls / a continuous tone below a second threshold / display showing distance.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Sensors and microprocessor control

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A water-treatment plant in Faisalabad must keep the pH of drinking water between 6.5 and 8.5. If the pH falls below 6.5 an alkali valve is opened; if it rises above 8.5 an acid valve is opened. An alarm sounds if the pH is outside 6.0–9.0.
Describe how a microprocessor-controlled system with a pH sensor would work.
parts.answer: The pH sensor sends readings continuously; ADC converts to digital; the microprocessor compares the reading with stored values; below 6.5 → signal to actuator to open the alkali valve; above 8.5 → open the acid valve; between 6.5 and 8.5 → both valves closed; if below 6.0 or above 9.0 the microprocessor also sends a signal to sound the alarm; the readings are checked again in a continuous loop.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: pH sensor sends data; analogue to digital conversion; comparison with stored values; < 6.5 opens alkali valve via actuator; > 8.5 opens acid valve; otherwise valves closed; < 6.0 or > 9.0 triggers alarm; continuous loop/regular intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons for using a microprocessor-controlled system instead of a worker who tests the water by hand.
parts.answer: Readings are taken continuously, including at night; responses are faster and more accurate; no human error or fatigue; safer for workers near chemicals.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: works 24/7; faster response; more accurate/consistent; no human error; safer; cheaper in the long term.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Network hardware and addressing (NIC, MAC, IP, router)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of a network interface card (NIC).
parts.answer: It allows a device to connect to a network.
parts.working: B1 provides a connection to a (wired or wireless) network; contains the MAC address.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: It connects the home network to the internet; it receives data packets and forwards them to the correct device using the IP address; it assigns local IP addresses to devices (DHCP).

parts.answer: A static IP address does not change; a dynamic IP address is assigned each time a device connects and may change. A web server needs a static address so that DNS records stay correct and users can always find it.
parts.working: 1 mark: static is permanent/does not change. 1 mark: dynamic is assigned (by the router/ISP) each connection and can change. 1 mark: server needs a fixed address so it can always be located / DNS maps to it reliably.

parts.answer: The MAC address is fixed by the manufacturer and identifies the device on the local network; the IP address identifies the device's location on a network/the internet and is used to route data between networks.
parts.working: 1 mark: MAC identifies the device physically / unique, set by manufacturer. 1 mark: IP is a logical address that identifies where the device is on the internet, used for routing.

subtopic: Lossy and lossless compression

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
parts.answer: Lossy compression permanently removes some data, so the original file cannot be recovered exactly; lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be restored exactly.
parts.working: 1 mark: lossy – data permanently removed, original cannot be restored. 1 mark: lossless – no data lost, original can be reconstructed exactly.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: (i) Lossless – every number must be exactly correct; any lost data would corrupt the file. (ii) Lossy – the photo can be made much smaller and the small loss of quality is not noticeable to viewers.
parts.working: Each part: 1 mark for the type, 1 mark for the reason.

parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: perceptual music shaping; removes frequencies outside the range of human hearing; removes quieter sounds masked by louder sounds; reduces sample rate; reduces sample resolution/bit depth; data removed permanently.

parts.label: b

parts.working: 1 mark each: reduce resolution / number of pixels; reduce colour depth. Accept: group similar colours together.

parts.answer: Smaller files stream faster and use less of the user's mobile data and storage.
parts.working: B1 faster download/streaming; less bandwidth/data used; less storage needed on the server or device.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Representing text, sound and images

parts.label: a

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why errors can occur when data is transmitted.
parts.answer: Electrical interference; data loss, gain or change caused by problems in the connection (e.g. a damaged cable or weak wireless signal).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: interference (electrical/electromagnetic); data loss; data gain; data change/corruption; poor connection or damaged cable; weak/obstructed wireless signal; packet collisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three methods that can be used to detect errors after data has been transmitted.
parts.answer: Parity check, checksum, echo check (also automatic repeat query).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: parity check (byte or block); checksum; echo check; ARQ.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A system uses even parity. The parity bit is the left-most bit. Write the complete 8-bit byte for each of these 7-bit data values:
(i) 1011001
(ii) 0110100
(iii) 1111111
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) four 1s → parity 0; (ii) three 1s → parity 1; (iii) seven 1s → parity 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by even parity.
parts.answer: The total number of 1s in the byte, including the parity bit, must be even.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A school's network uses odd parity. These four bytes are received:
Byte 1: 10110011
Byte 2: 01101100
Byte 3: 11100000
Byte 4: 00011101
Identify which bytes have been received with an error. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Byte 2 (four 1s) and Byte 4 (four 1s) – each has an even number of 1s, so it fails the odd parity check.
parts.working: 1 mark: byte 2; 1 mark: byte 4; 1 mark: reason – an even number of 1s when odd parity is used (bytes 1 and 3 each have five or three 1s, which is odd).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Byte 3 passed the parity check but was still incorrect. Explain how this is possible.
parts.answer: If two bits (an even number of bits) are changed during transmission, the number of 1s stays odd, so the parity check cannot detect the error.
parts.working: 1 mark: two/an even number of bits changed. 1 mark: parity is unchanged so the error is not detected.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Six bytes of data were sent using even parity, with a parity block. The left-most bit of each byte is its parity bit, and the final row is the parity byte (it gives even parity for each column). The data received is:
Byte 1: 0 1 0 1 1 0 0 1
Byte 2: 0 0 1 1 0 1 1 0
Byte 3: 0 1 1 1 0 0 0 1
Byte 4: 1 0 0 0 1 1 1 1
Byte 5: 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 0
Byte 6: 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 1
Parity byte: 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 0
One bit has been changed during transmission. Identify the byte and the bit position (1 = left-most) of the error, and explain how you found it.
parts.answer: Byte 4, bit position 6. Byte 4 has five 1s (odd) so the error is in that row; column 6 contains an odd number of 1s (including the parity byte) so the error is in that column; the bit where they cross is wrong (it should be 0).
parts.working: 1 mark: byte 4. 1 mark: bit position 6. 1 mark: row with odd number of 1s identified. 1 mark: column with odd number of 1s identified / intersection gives the bit, which is then flipped to correct it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a parity block over a single parity bit per byte.
parts.answer: It can locate exactly which bit is wrong, so the error can be corrected without resending the data.
parts.working: B1 identifies the position of the error / can correct a single-bit error.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a checksum is used to detect errors in transmitted data.
parts.answer: Before sending, a value (checksum) is calculated from the data using an agreed algorithm; the checksum is sent with the data; the receiver recalculates the checksum from the data it receives using the same algorithm; if the two checksums are different an error has occurred and the data is requested again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: checksum calculated from the block of data before sending; transmitted with the data; recalculated by the receiver using the same algorithm; compared – if they do not match, an error is detected / retransmission requested.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A device calculates its checksum as the total of the data values MOD 256. It sends these values: 156, 201, 77, 98, 240. Calculate the checksum. Show your working.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The receiver gets 156, 201, 77, 89, 240 and the checksum 4. Explain whether the error will be detected.
parts.answer: Yes – the receiver's total is 763, and 763 MOD 256 = 251, which does not match 4.
parts.working: B1 detected because recalculated checksum 251 ≠ 4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an echo check works.
parts.answer: The data is sent to the receiver; the receiver sends a copy of the data back to the sender; the sender compares the returned copy with the original; if they are different an error has occurred and the data is sent again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: data sent; receiver returns the data to the sender; sender compares the two copies; if different, error detected and data resent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of an echo check.
parts.answer: It is not known whether the error happened on the way to the receiver or on the way back; it doubles the amount of data transmitted.
parts.working: B1 cannot tell in which direction the error occurred / doubles transmission time or traffic.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online banking app in Islamabad uses an automatic repeat query (ARQ). Describe how ARQ ensures that data arrives correctly.
parts.answer: The receiver checks the data using an error-detection method; if correct it sends a positive acknowledgement; if an error is found it sends a negative acknowledgement and the sender resends the data; the sender starts a timer (timeout) when it sends, and if no acknowledgement arrives before the timeout it resends automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: receiver uses an error check (e.g. parity/checksum); positive acknowledgement sent if no error; negative acknowledgement if error; sender resends on negative acknowledgement; timeout starts when data sent; data resent if no acknowledgement before timeout; repeats until received correctly (or a set number of tries).

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite sends large blocks of scientific data to a ground station in Pakistan. It takes the signal a long time to travel. Compare the suitability of an echo check and a checksum for this link.
parts.answer: An echo check doubles the transmission (all the data must be sent back), which would be very slow over a long-delay link; the error could also occur on the return journey. A checksum adds only a small value to each block, so little extra data is sent; the ground station can check each block itself and request only the faulty blocks again. So a checksum (with ARQ) is more suitable.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: echo check sends all data back – doubles traffic/time; long delay makes echo check slow; error may occur on return so ambiguous; checksum adds little extra data; receiver can check without returning data; only faulty blocks resent; conclusion that checksum is more suitable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a parity check on each byte would be less reliable than a checksum for this data.
parts.answer: A parity check cannot detect an even number of bit errors in a byte, and with noisy signals several bits may change; a checksum based on the whole block is more likely to detect such errors.
parts.working: 1 mark: parity misses errors where an even number of bits change. 1 mark: checksum covers the whole block / more likely to detect multiple errors.

subtopic: Transmission methods (serial/parallel, simplex/duplex, USB)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why serial transmission is used for long-distance connections even though parallel transmission sends more bits at once.
parts.answer: In parallel transmission the bits travel along separate wires and can arrive at slightly different times (skewing), which becomes worse over long distances and corrupts the data; serial transmission uses one wire so bits arrive in order with no skew; it is also cheaper because fewer wires are needed and suffers less interference (crosstalk).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: parallel bits can become skewed / arrive out of sync; skew increases with distance; serial has no skew – bits arrive in order; serial needs fewer wires so cheaper; less crosstalk/interference with one wire; serial more reliable over distance.

parts.answer: Over very short distances, such as inside the computer between the CPU and memory (internal buses).
parts.working: B1 internal buses / within an integrated circuit / very short connection.

(ii) Data is moved between the CPU and memory inside a laptop.

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how symmetric encryption is used to send a message securely.
parts.answer: The sender uses a key and an encryption algorithm to turn the plaintext into ciphertext; the ciphertext is sent; the receiver uses the same key to decrypt the ciphertext back into plaintext.
parts.working: 1 mark each: plaintext encrypted using a key/algorithm; ciphertext transmitted; same key used to decrypt.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A cricket academy in Sialkot records the runs scored by its 20 players in each of 10 matches. The program uses:
• a one-dimensional array PlayerName[1:20] of type STRING, already holding the players' names
• a two-dimensional array Runs[1:20, 1:10] of type INTEGER
Requirements:
• allow the runs for every player in every match to be input, rejecting any value below 0 or above 300
• calculate each player's total and average runs (average rounded to 1 decimal place) and output the name, total and average
• find and output the name of the player with the highest total.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section of the program that inputs and validates the runs for every player in every match.
parts.answer:
FOR Player ← 1 TO 20
    FOR Match ← 1 TO 10
        OUTPUT "Enter runs for ", PlayerName[Player], " in match ", Match
        INPUT Runs[Player, Match]
        WHILE Runs[Player, Match] < 0 OR Runs[Player, Match] > 300 DO
            OUTPUT "Invalid: runs must be 0 to 300. Re-enter"
            INPUT Runs[Player, Match]
        ENDWHILE
    NEXT Match
NEXT Player
parts.working: 1 mark each: outer loop for 20 players; inner loop for 10 matches; prompt and input into Runs[Player, Match]; validation condition < 0 OR > 300; re-input with error message inside a loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and outputs each player's total and average.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Average : REAL
FOR Player ← 1 TO 20
    Total ← 0
    FOR Match ← 1 TO 10
        Total ← Total + Runs[Player, Match]
    NEXT Match
    Average ← ROUND(Total / 10, 1)
    OUTPUT PlayerName[Player], " total: ", Total, " average: ", Average
NEXT Player
parts.working: 1 mark each: loop through players; total reset to 0 for each player; inner loop adds Runs[Player, Match]; average = total / 10 rounded to 1 d.p.; output name, total and average with messages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that finds and outputs the name of the player with the highest total. (You may store each total in an array Totals[1:20] in part (b).)
parts.answer:
// assumes Totals[Player] ← Total was added inside the loop in (b)
DECLARE Highest : INTEGER
DECLARE BestPlayer : INTEGER
Highest ← Totals[1]
BestPlayer ← 1
FOR Player ← 2 TO 20
    IF Totals[Player] > Highest THEN
        Highest ← Totals[Player]
        BestPlayer ← Player
    ENDIF
NEXT Player
OUTPUT "Highest scorer: ", PlayerName[BestPlayer], " with ", Highest, " runs"
parts.working: 1 mark each: totals stored in an array (or recalculated); highest initialised to first total (or −1); loop compares each total with highest; highest and index updated together; output name of best player using the stored index with message.

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A power company calculates monthly bills for 50 households. Each household's meter reading at the start and end of the month is input. Units used = end reading − start reading.
Charges:
• the first 100 units cost Rs 10 each
• units from 101 to 300 cost Rs 15 each
• every unit above 300 costs Rs 25
The program uses arrays HouseID[1:50] (STRING, already filled) and Bill[1:50] (REAL).
Requirements:
• input both readings for each house; the end reading must not be less than the start reading
• calculate and store each bill, and output the house ID with its units and bill
• output the total of all bills and the number of households that used more than 300 units.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates both readings for one household and calculates the units used.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Start reading for ", HouseID[House]
INPUT StartReading
OUTPUT "End reading for ", HouseID[House]
INPUT EndReading
WHILE EndReading < StartReading DO
    OUTPUT "End reading cannot be less than start reading. Re-enter end reading"
    INPUT EndReading
ENDWHILE
Units ← EndReading − StartReading
parts.working: 1 mark each: inputs with prompts; validation condition EndReading < StartReading; loop with error message and re-input; units calculated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates the bill for one household from Units and stores it in Bill[House].
parts.answer:
IF Units <= 100 THEN
    Bill[House] ← Units * 10
ELSE
    IF Units <= 300 THEN
        Bill[House] ← 100 * 10 + (Units − 100) * 15
    ELSE
        Bill[House] ← 100 * 10 + 200 * 15 + (Units − 300) * 25
        Over300 ← Over300 + 1
    ENDIF
ENDIF
OUTPUT HouseID[House], " units: ", Units, " bill: Rs ", Bill[House]
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: correct first band (≤ 100 × 10); correct condition for second band; second band = 1000 + (Units − 100) × 15; third band = 1000 + 3000 + (Units − 300) × 25; count of households over 300 incremented; output of ID, units and bill.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the rest of the program: the loop for all 50 households, initialising the counters, and outputting the total of all bills and the count of households above 300 units. (Use your sections from (a) and (b).)
parts.answer:
DECLARE TotalBills : REAL
DECLARE Over300 : INTEGER
TotalBills ← 0
Over300 ← 0
FOR House ← 1 TO 50
    // section (a)
    // section (b)
    TotalBills ← TotalBills + Bill[House]
NEXT House
OUTPUT "Total of all bills: Rs ", TotalBills
OUTPUT "Households using more than 300 units: ", Over300
parts.working: 1 mark each: totals and counter initialised to 0 before the loop; loop 1 to 50 around (a) and (b); running total updated inside the loop; total output after the loop; count output after the loop with message.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the bill for a household that uses 350 units.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A cinema in Hyderabad has 8 rows (A to H, numbered 1 to 8 in the program) with 12 seats in each row. The program uses a two-dimensional Boolean array Booked[1:8, 1:12], where TRUE means the seat is taken. A ticket costs Rs 900, but seats in rows 1 and 2 cost Rs 600.
Requirements:
• at the start, set every seat to not booked
• repeatedly let a customer choose a row and seat number; validate both; if the seat is free, book it and add the price to the takings, otherwise output a message
• stop when the customer enters 0 for the row
• at the end, output the total takings and the number of empty seats in each row.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that sets every seat to not booked and initialises the takings.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Booked : ARRAY[1:8, 1:12] OF BOOLEAN
DECLARE Takings : INTEGER
Takings ← 0
FOR Row ← 1 TO 8
    FOR Seat ← 1 TO 12
        Booked[Row, Seat] ← FALSE
    NEXT Seat
NEXT Row
parts.working: 1 mark each: nested loops over 8 rows and 12 seats; each element set to FALSE; takings initialised to 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that handles bookings until 0 is entered for the row.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Enter row number (1-8), or 0 to finish"
INPUT Row
WHILE Row <> 0 DO
    IF Row < 1 OR Row > 8 THEN
        OUTPUT "Invalid row"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Enter seat number (1-12)"
        INPUT Seat
        WHILE Seat < 1 OR Seat > 12 DO
            OUTPUT "Invalid seat, re-enter (1-12)"
            INPUT Seat
        ENDWHILE
        IF Booked[Row, Seat] = TRUE THEN
            OUTPUT "Sorry, that seat is already booked"
        ELSE
            Booked[Row, Seat] ← TRUE
            IF Row <= 2 THEN
                Takings ← Takings + 600
            ELSE
                Takings ← Takings + 900
            ENDIF
            OUTPUT "Seat booked"
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT "Enter row number (1-8), or 0 to finish"
    INPUT Row
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each: condition-controlled loop ending when row = 0; row validated (1–8); seat input and validated (1–12); check Booked[Row, Seat] before booking; seat set to TRUE; correct price added (600 for rows 1–2, otherwise 900); messages for taken seat/invalid input and re-input of row inside the loop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the total takings and the number of empty seats in each row.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Total takings: Rs ", Takings
FOR Row ← 1 TO 8
    Empty ← 0
    FOR Seat ← 1 TO 12
        IF Booked[Row, Seat] = FALSE THEN
            Empty ← Empty + 1
        ENDIF
    NEXT Seat
    OUTPUT "Row ", Row, ": ", Empty, " empty seats"
NEXT Row
parts.working: 1 mark each: takings output with message; loop through rows; counter reset for each row; counts seats that are FALSE; outputs row number and count.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A school canteen sells 5 items. The arrays ItemName[1:5] (STRING) and Price[1:5] (REAL) already hold the item names and prices. An array Sold[1:5] of INTEGER will hold the number of each item sold in a day.
Requirements:
• set all values in Sold to 0
• for each order, display a numbered menu, input the item number (1–5) and quantity (1–10) with validation, output the cost of that order and update Sold
• stop taking orders when the item number 9 is entered
• output, for each item, the name, number sold and money taken, and then the total money taken for the day.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that initialises Sold and displays the menu.
parts.answer:
FOR Item ← 1 TO 5
    Sold[Item] ← 0
NEXT Item
// menu display (used before each order)
FOR Item ← 1 TO 5
    OUTPUT Item, " ", ItemName[Item], " Rs ", Price[Item]
NEXT Item
OUTPUT "9 Finish for the day"
parts.working: 1 mark each: loop setting Sold[1..5] to 0; loop outputting number, name and price; option to finish shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that takes orders until 9 is entered.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Enter item number"
INPUT Choice
WHILE Choice <> 9 DO
    IF Choice >= 1 AND Choice <= 5 THEN
        OUTPUT "Enter quantity (1-10)"
        INPUT Quantity
        WHILE Quantity < 1 OR Quantity > 10 DO
            OUTPUT "Quantity must be 1 to 10"
            INPUT Quantity
        ENDWHILE
        OUTPUT "Cost: Rs ", Quantity * Price[Choice]
        Sold[Choice] ← Sold[Choice] + Quantity
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Invalid item number"
    ENDIF
    // display menu again (section a)
    OUTPUT "Enter item number"
    INPUT Choice
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each: loop ending when 9 entered; item number validated 1–5; quantity input; quantity validated 1–10 in a loop; cost = quantity × Price[Choice] output; Sold[Choice] increased by quantity; new item number input inside the loop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the daily summary.
parts.answer:
DayTotal ← 0
FOR Item ← 1 TO 5
    Money ← Sold[Item] * Price[Item]
    OUTPUT ItemName[Item], ": ", Sold[Item], " sold, Rs ", Money
    DayTotal ← DayTotal + Money
NEXT Item
OUTPUT "Total for the day: Rs ", DayTotal
parts.working: 1 mark each: total initialised; loop over 5 items; money per item = Sold × Price; output name, number sold and money; day total accumulated and output after loop.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A public library in Peshawar records returned books. For each of 30 returns in a day, the librarian inputs the member ID (exactly 6 characters) and the number of days late (0 to 60). The fine is Rs 20 per day for the first 7 days late and Rs 50 per day after that; the maximum fine is Rs 2000.
The program uses arrays MemberID[1:30] (STRING) and Fine[1:30] (INTEGER).
Requirements:
• input and validate the member ID (length check) and days late (range check)
• calculate and store each fine and output it
• output the total fines, the average fine of the members who paid a fine (rounded to 2 decimal places), and the member ID with the largest fine.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates the data for return number Count.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Enter 6-character member ID"
INPUT MemberID[Count]
WHILE LENGTH(MemberID[Count]) <> 6 DO
    OUTPUT "ID must be exactly 6 characters. Re-enter"
    INPUT MemberID[Count]
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "Enter days late (0-60)"
INPUT DaysLate
WHILE DaysLate < 0 OR DaysLate > 60 DO
    OUTPUT "Days late must be 0 to 60. Re-enter"
    INPUT DaysLate
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ID input into array; length check using LENGTH() <> 6; re-input loop with message; days late input; range check 0–60 with re-input loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and stores the fine for return number Count.
parts.answer:
IF DaysLate <= 7 THEN
    Fine[Count] ← DaysLate * 20
ELSE
    Fine[Count] ← 7 * 20 + (DaysLate − 7) * 50
ENDIF
IF Fine[Count] > 2000 THEN
    Fine[Count] ← 2000
ENDIF
OUTPUT "Fine for ", MemberID[Count], ": Rs ", Fine[Count]
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: condition DaysLate <= 7; fine = days × 20; fine = 140 + (days − 7) × 50; capped at 2000; output of fine with ID.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the total, the average fine of members who paid a fine, and the member with the largest fine.
parts.answer:
Total ← 0
Payers ← 0
MaxIndex ← 1
FOR Count ← 1 TO 30
    Total ← Total + Fine[Count]
    IF Fine[Count] > 0 THEN
        Payers ← Payers + 1
    ENDIF
    IF Fine[Count] > Fine[MaxIndex] THEN
        MaxIndex ← Count
    ENDIF
NEXT Count
OUTPUT "Total fines: Rs ", Total
IF Payers > 0 THEN
    OUTPUT "Average fine: Rs ", ROUND(Total / Payers, 2)
ELSE
    OUTPUT "No fines today"
ENDIF
OUTPUT "Largest fine: ", MemberID[MaxIndex], " Rs ", Fine[MaxIndex]
parts.working: 1 mark each: total accumulated; payers counted only when fine > 0; average = total / payers rounded to 2 d.p. (division by zero avoided); index of largest fine tracked; outputs with messages.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the fines for members who are 20 days late and 45 days late.
parts.answer: Rs 790 and Rs 2000

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A charity marathon in Lahore has up to 500 runners. Each runner's number (1 to 500) and finishing time in hours, minutes and seconds are input. The program stores the times in seconds in an array Seconds[1:500] of INTEGER; a value of 0 means the runner did not finish.
Requirements:
• set every element of Seconds to 0
• input results until runner number −1 is entered; validate the runner number, minutes and seconds (0–59) and hours (0–7); a runner number that already has a time must be rejected
• output the number of finishers, the runner number of the fastest finisher and the average finishing time as hours, minutes and whole seconds
• output how many finishers completed in under 4 hours.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that initialises the array and inputs and validates all results.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Seconds : ARRAY[1:500] OF INTEGER
FOR R ← 1 TO 500
    Seconds[R] ← 0
NEXT R
OUTPUT "Enter runner number (-1 to finish)"
INPUT Runner
WHILE Runner <> -1 DO
    IF Runner < 1 OR Runner > 500 THEN
        OUTPUT "Invalid runner number"
    ELSE
        IF Seconds[Runner] <> 0 THEN
            OUTPUT "This runner already has a time"
        ELSE
            REPEAT
                OUTPUT "Enter hours, minutes, seconds"
                INPUT H, M, S
            UNTIL H >= 0 AND H <= 7 AND M >= 0 AND M <= 59 AND S >= 0 AND S <= 59
            Seconds[Runner] ← H * 3600 + M * 60 + S
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT "Enter runner number (-1 to finish)"
    INPUT Runner
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: array initialised to 0; loop until −1; runner number range checked; duplicate check (Seconds[Runner] <> 0); hours, minutes, seconds input; validation of all three ranges with re-input; conversion H × 3600 + M × 60 + S; stored at Seconds[Runner] and next runner input inside loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and outputs the number of finishers, the fastest runner and the count under 4 hours.
parts.answer:
Finishers ← 0
Total ← 0
Fastest ← 0
Under4 ← 0
FOR R ← 1 TO 500
    IF Seconds[R] > 0 THEN
        Finishers ← Finishers + 1
        Total ← Total + Seconds[R]
        IF Fastest = 0 THEN
            Fastest ← R
        ELSE
            IF Seconds[R] < Seconds[Fastest] THEN
                Fastest ← R
            ENDIF
        ENDIF
        IF Seconds[R] < 4 * 3600 THEN
            Under4 ← Under4 + 1
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
NEXT R
OUTPUT "Finishers: ", Finishers
OUTPUT "Fastest runner: ", Fastest
OUTPUT "Under 4 hours: ", Under4
parts.working: 1 mark each: only times > 0 counted; fastest found correctly (index stored, first finisher handled); under-4-hours test uses 14 400 seconds; outputs with messages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the average finishing time in hours, minutes and whole seconds.
parts.answer:
IF Finishers > 0 THEN
    Avg ← ROUND(Total / Finishers, 0)
    OUTPUT "Average: ", Avg DIV 3600, " h ", (Avg MOD 3600) DIV 60, " min ", Avg MOD 60, " s"
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark each: average = total ÷ finishers rounded to whole seconds (division by zero avoided); hours using DIV 3600; minutes and seconds using MOD/DIV.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The average time is 15 125 seconds. State what your program outputs for the average.
parts.answer: Average: 4 h 12 min 5 s

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A cold-storage warehouse near Okara stores mangoes for export. A temperature reading (°C, REAL) is taken every hour for 7 days and stored in a two-dimensional array Temp[1:7, 1:24]. Safe readings are from 8.0 to 13.0 inclusive.
Requirements:
• input all 168 readings; any reading below −10 or above 40 must be rejected as a sensor fault and re-entered
• for each day output the day number, the lowest and highest reading and the average reading to 1 decimal place
• output the day and hour of every unsafe reading
• output 'SPOILAGE RISK' for any day that has 3 or more consecutive unsafe readings.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates all the readings.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        REPEAT
            OUTPUT "Temperature for day ", Day, " hour ", Hour
            INPUT Temp[Day, Hour]
        UNTIL Temp[Day, Hour] >= -10 AND Temp[Day, Hour] <= 40
    NEXT Hour
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: nested loops 7 × 24; prompt and input to Temp[Day, Hour]; validation −10 to 40; re-input until valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that outputs each day's lowest, highest and average reading, and the day and hour of every unsafe reading.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    Low ← Temp[Day, 1]
    High ← Temp[Day, 1]
    DayTotal ← 0
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        DayTotal ← DayTotal + Temp[Day, Hour]
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < Low THEN
            Low ← Temp[Day, Hour]
        ENDIF
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] > High THEN
            High ← Temp[Day, Hour]
        ENDIF
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < 8.0 OR Temp[Day, Hour] > 13.0 THEN
            OUTPUT "Unsafe reading on day ", Day, " at hour ", Hour
        ENDIF
    NEXT Hour
    OUTPUT "Day ", Day, " low ", Low, " high ", High, " average ", ROUND(DayTotal / 24, 1)
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: low and high initialised to first reading of the day; sum reset per day; comparisons update low and high; average = sum / 24 rounded to 1 d.p.; unsafe test < 8.0 OR > 13.0; outputs day and hour of unsafe readings; daily output with messages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs 'SPOILAGE RISK' for any day with 3 or more consecutive unsafe readings.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    Run ← 0
    Risk ← FALSE
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < 8.0 OR Temp[Day, Hour] > 13.0 THEN
            Run ← Run + 1
            IF Run >= 3 THEN
                Risk ← TRUE
            ENDIF
        ELSE
            Run ← 0
        ENDIF
    NEXT Hour
    IF Risk = TRUE THEN
        OUTPUT "Day ", Day, ": SPOILAGE RISK"
    ENDIF
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: counter of consecutive unsafe readings increased; counter reset to 0 on a safe reading; flag set when counter reaches 3 (output only once per day); output with day number.
