parts.working: 1 mark for C; 1 mark for explanation using the expression/truth table.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Logic gate symbols and truth tables
stem: An XOR gate has inputs A and B and output X.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the truth table for X for all combinations of inputs A, B.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct row.

parts.label: b

parts.text: Write pseudocode that uses a REPEAT … UNTIL loop to input the number of chairs ordered for a wedding hall. The number must be a whole number from 1 to 50 inclusive. Output a suitable message each time an invalid number is entered. You may use ROUND(Value, 0), which returns Value rounded to 0 decimal places.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Chairs : REAL
REPEAT
   OUTPUT "Enter number of chairs (1 to 50)"
   INPUT Chairs
   IF Chairs < 1 OR Chairs > 50 OR ROUND(Chairs, 0) <> Chairs THEN
      OUTPUT "Invalid – whole number 1 to 50 only"
   ENDIF
UNTIL Chairs >= 1 AND Chairs <= 50 AND ROUND(Chairs, 0) = Chairs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pakistani postal codes have exactly 5 digits, for example 54000. Write pseudocode that inputs a postal code as a STRING and outputs "Accepted" if it is exactly 5 characters long and every character is a digit; otherwise it outputs "Rejected". You may use LENGTH(String) and SUBSTRING(String, Start, Length).
parts.answer:
DECLARE Code : STRING
DECLARE Valid : BOOLEAN
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Ch : CHAR
INPUT Code
Valid ← TRUE
IF LENGTH(Code) <> 5 THEN
   Valid ← FALSE
ELSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
      Ch ← SUBSTRING(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < "0" OR Ch > "9" THEN
         Valid ← FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
ENDIF
IF Valid = TRUE THEN
   OUTPUT "Accepted"
ELSE
   OUTPUT "Rejected"
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark: input as string; 1 mark: length check = 5; 1 mark: loop through each character; 1 mark: SUBSTRING to extract one character; 1 mark: test character between "0" and "9" and set a flag; 1 mark: correct output based on flag.

parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsLeap(Year : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   IF MOD(Year, 400) = 0 THEN
      RETURN TRUE
   ELSE
      IF MOD(Year, 100) = 0 THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ELSE
         IF MOD(Year, 4) = 0 THEN
            RETURN TRUE
         ELSE
            RETURN FALSE
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

      ENDIF
   ENDIF
NEXT Q
IF Score < 0 THEN
   Score ← 0
ENDIF
OUTPUT "Score: ", Score

• outputs "Member at position" and the position, or "Not a member".
parts.answer:
DECLARE ID : STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Found : BOOLEAN
INPUT ID
Index ← 0
Found ← FALSE

ELSE

ENDIF

parts.label: a

parts.answer:
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE TempScore : INTEGER
DECLARE TempName : STRING
DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
REPEAT
   Swapped ← FALSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 24
      IF Scores[Index] < Scores[Index + 1] THEN
         TempScore ← Scores[Index]
         Scores[Index] ← Scores[Index + 1]
         Scores[Index + 1] ← TempScore
         TempName ← Names[Index]
         Names[Index] ← Names[Index + 1]
         Names[Index + 1] ← TempName
         Swapped ← TRUE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
UNTIL Swapped = FALSE
parts.working: 1 mark: outer loop repeating until no swaps; 1 mark: inner loop 1 to 24; 1 mark: comparison < for descending order; 1 mark: swap of scores using a temporary variable; 1 mark: matching swap of names; 1 mark: flag set/reset correctly.

parts.answer:
DECLARE Value : INTEGER
DECLARE Total, Valid, Rejected : INTEGER
Total ← 0
Valid ← 0
Rejected ← 0
INPUT Value
WHILE Value <> -1
   IF Value >= 0 AND Value <= 100 THEN
      Total ← Total + Value
      Valid ← Valid + 1
   ELSE
      Rejected ← Rejected + 1
   ENDIF
   INPUT Value
ENDWHILE
IF Valid > 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / Valid
ENDIF
OUTPUT "Rejected: ", Rejected
parts.working: 1 mark: initialise total and both counters; 1 mark: input before loop and again at the end of the loop; 1 mark: WHILE loop ends on -1 (which is not counted); 1 mark: range test 0 to 100 with totalling and counting; 1 mark: count rejected values; 1 mark: average = total ÷ valid count, avoiding division by zero, and outputs.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student is writing a program in an integrated development environment (IDE). Describe the purpose of each IDE feature.
(i) Prettyprint
(ii) Code completion
(iii) Error diagnostics
(iv) Run-time environment
parts.answer: (i) Colour-codes keywords and indents code so it is easier to read. (ii) Suggests or completes keywords, variable names and statement structures as the code is typed, which saves typing and reduces errors. (iii) Identifies errors and shows where they are, with messages explaining them. (iv) Lets the program be run inside the IDE so its behaviour can be tested and observed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A program contains a loop that is repeated 1 000 000 times. Explain why the program runs more slowly when it is interpreted than when it is compiled.
parts.answer: An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time, every time it is reached, so the statements in the loop are translated 1 000 000 times. A compiler translates the whole program once into machine code before it runs, so the loop runs as machine code with no translation during execution.
parts.working: 1 mark: interpreter translates line by line each time the line is executed; 1 mark: loop body re-translated on every repetition; 1 mark: compiled code is translated once, in advance, and executes directly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the programmer may still prefer to use the interpreter while developing this program.
parts.answer: It stops at the first error and reports it immediately, so errors can be found and corrected one at a time; the program can be run without translating it all first.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.answer: System software that helps maintain, optimise or protect the computer (e.g. keeps it running efficiently and securely).
parts.working: 1 mark.

(i) Deciding which part of RAM a newly opened program will use
(ii) Asking a user for a username and password before allowing access
(iii) Letting a user create folders and rename files

parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: An operating system provides an interface for the user. Describe the difference between a graphical user interface (GUI) and a command line interface (CLI).
parts.answer: A GUI uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP) so the user clicks or taps; a CLI requires the user to type commands as text.
parts.working: 1 mark: GUI uses icons/menus/pointer; 1 mark: CLI uses typed commands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which interface is more suitable for a person using a computer for the first time, and which might be preferred by a network technician. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: First-time user: GUI – easy to learn, no commands to remember. Technician: CLI – direct, fast control and can run scripts/commands not available from menus, uses fewer resources.
parts.working: 1 mark each with a reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.text: A family shares one laptop. Explain how the operating system manages separate user accounts for each family member.
parts.answer: The OS lets an administrator create an account for each person with its own username and password; each user has their own files, desktop and settings; access rights stop one user from opening or deleting another user's files or changing system settings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: separate login with password; own private files/folders; own settings/preferences; access rights/permissions set by an administrator account.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photographer in Skardu stores thousands of photos on a laptop. Describe three ways in which the operating system's file management helps her organise her work.
parts.answer: She can create a folder structure (e.g. a folder per trip); she can name, rename, copy, move and delete files; the OS records where each file is stored on the drive so she can open and search for it by name; she can see file properties such as size and date.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three file-management operations or features applied to the scenario.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has a spreadsheet and a web browser open at the same time. Explain how the operating system's memory management stops the two programs interfering with each other.
parts.answer: The OS allocates each program its own separate area of RAM; it keeps track of which areas are in use; it stops a program reading or writing memory allocated to the other (memory protection); it frees the memory when a program is closed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each task, name the most suitable type of application software and give a reason.
(i) Calculating the monthly budget of a charity, with totals that update automatically
(ii) Storing and searching the records of 5000 library books
(iii) Writing a formatted letter to parents
(iv) Showing a slide show about a science project to the class
parts.answer: (i) Spreadsheet – formulas recalculate automatically. (ii) Database – stores records in fields and can search/sort/query them. (iii) Word processor – text formatting, templates, spell check. (iv) Presentation software – slides, transitions, displayed to an audience.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the software type with a suitable reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user double-clicks the icon of a drawing app on a laptop. Explain the role of the operating system from that moment until the app's window appears on screen.
parts.answer: The mouse click causes an interrupt, which the OS handles. Through file management the OS finds the app's program file on secondary storage. Memory management allocates space in RAM and the program is loaded into it. The OS schedules the program so the processor gives it time (process/multitasking management). The OS then displays the app's window through its user interface and manages its input/output.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: handles the click as an interrupt; locates the file on storage (file management); allocates RAM and loads the program (memory management); allocates processor time/manages multitasking; provides the platform for the app to run; shows the window via the user interface.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: The microwave oven in a kitchen in Karachi is controlled by a microprocessor running a single program stored in ROM. Explain why it does not need a full operating system like a laptop, and why it still needs software.
parts.answer: It performs only one dedicated task, so there is no need to manage multiple applications, users, files or a wide range of peripherals; it has limited memory and processing power, which a full OS would waste. It still needs firmware (the control program) to read the keypad and sensors and to control the magnetron, turntable and display.
parts.working: 1 mark: single dedicated task/no multitasking; 1 mark: no file or user management needed/limited resources; 1 mark: still needs a control program (firmware) stored in ROM; 1 mark: the program processes inputs and controls outputs.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scanner is plugged into a USB port of an office computer while a 30-page document is being printed. Explain how the operating system deals with both devices.
parts.answer: The OS detects the new device (an interrupt) and identifies it, then loads/installs the correct device driver so it can communicate with the scanner. The printer continues to be managed through its own driver; data waiting to print is held in a buffer/queue. The OS handles interrupts from both devices (e.g. printer buffer empty, scan complete) and shares processor time between the tasks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: detects new device via interrupt; loads the correct driver; printer data queued/buffered; handles interrupts from each device; multitasking shares processor time; reports errors to the user (e.g. paper out).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company still uses computers with an operating system that no longer receives updates from its developer. Explain two risks of this, and suggest what the company should do.
parts.answer: 1. Security: newly discovered weaknesses are not patched, so malware and hackers can exploit them. 2. Compatibility: new application software and new hardware drivers may not be made for the old OS, so programs/devices stop working. The company should upgrade to a supported OS (or replace the computers), and meanwhile use a firewall, anti-malware and limit internet access for those machines.
parts.working: 2 marks for each risk (identification + explanation); 1 mark for a sensible action.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three different examples of events that cause a hardware interrupt.
parts.answer: e.g. a key is pressed on the keyboard; the mouse is moved or clicked; the printer runs out of paper; data arrives at the network card; a USB device is plugged in.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hardware-based events.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of events that cause a software interrupt.
parts.answer: e.g. a program tries to divide by zero; two processes try to use the same memory location; a program requests a service from the OS (such as reading a file); a program tries to access memory it is not allowed to use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an interrupt service routine (ISR).
parts.answer: A small program (set of instructions) that is run by the processor to handle a particular interrupt.
parts.working: 1 mark: program/code; 1 mark: run to deal with/handle a specific interrupt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one action that could be carried out by the ISR for the interrupt 'printer out of paper'.
parts.answer: Display a message to the user asking them to add paper (and pause the print job).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify whether each event causes a hardware interrupt or a software interrupt.
(i) A user taps the touch screen of a tablet
(ii) A calculator app attempts to divide 45 by 0
(iii) A webcam is unplugged
(iv) A game asks the operating system to save a file
(v) A paper jam occurs in a printer
parts.answer: (i) Hardware (ii) Software (iii) Hardware (iv) Software (v) Hardware
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each interrupt is given a priority. State what is meant by interrupt priority.
parts.answer: A value showing how urgent the interrupt is, which decides the order in which interrupts are handled.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where interrupts are held while they are waiting to be serviced.
parts.answer: In an interrupt queue (in priority order).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the paragraph using words from the list. Not all words are used.
List: priority, register, queue, service routine, compiler, fetch-decode-execute, ignore
When a device needs attention it sends an interrupt signal to the processor. The interrupt is placed in a …(1)… . At the end of each …(2)… cycle the processor checks for interrupts. If the interrupt has a higher …(3)… than the current task, the processor saves its current state and runs the interrupt …(4)… .
parts.answer: (1) queue (2) fetch-decode-execute (3) priority (4) service routine
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A spreadsheet formula tries to divide a value by a cell that contains 0. Explain why this causes a software interrupt and what happens next.
parts.answer: Division by zero cannot be carried out, so the processor/program generates an interrupt to signal an error. The current task is paused and the ISR for this error runs, which stops the calculation and reports an error (e.g. an error message in the cell) instead of the program crashing; the program then continues.
parts.working: 1 mark: division by zero is an impossible operation/error detected by software; 1 mark: interrupt handled by an ISR; 1 mark: error reported and normal processing resumes.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The steps taken when an interrupt is handled are listed below in the wrong order. Write them in the correct order, using the letters.
A The ISR for the interrupt is run
B The interrupt signal is sent and placed in the queue
C The state of the current task is restored and it continues
D The processor checks the queue at the end of the current cycle
E The current task's register contents are saved
parts.answer: B, D, E, A, C
parts.working: 4 marks all correct; 3 marks for four in the correct relative order; 2 marks for three; 1 mark for B first or C last.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Rawalpindi prints a 40-page report. The printer runs out of paper after page 25. Describe how interrupts are used in this situation, from the moment the paper runs out until printing finishes.
parts.answer: The printer sends an interrupt to the processor. The processor saves its current task and runs the ISR, which displays an 'out of paper' message; printing of the remaining pages is paused. When paper is added, the printer sends another interrupt signal, and the OS resumes sending the remaining 15 pages; other work carries on meanwhile.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: printer sends interrupt; processor services it (saves state, runs ISR); user alerted; print job paused/data kept in buffer; new interrupt when paper added; printing resumes; processor does other tasks in between.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why interrupts are given different priorities. Use the examples of a power-failure warning from the power supply and a key press on the keyboard.
parts.answer: Some events are more urgent than others. A power-failure warning must be handled first, so data can be saved before the computer switches off; a key press can wait a few milliseconds without any harm, so it has a lower priority and is serviced later.
parts.working: 1 mark: interrupts differ in urgency/order of handling; 1 mark: power failure highest – data loss otherwise; 1 mark: key press low priority – delay unnoticed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain when and how the processor checks for interrupts during the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
parts.answer: At the end of each cycle (after an instruction is executed), the processor checks the interrupt queue/register. If there is an interrupt with a higher priority than the current task, it is serviced before the next instruction is fetched; otherwise the next instruction is fetched as normal.
parts.working: 1 mark: checked at the end of every cycle/after each instruction; 1 mark: compares priority with the current task; 1 mark: services it or continues with the next fetch.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A player presses the jump button on a games console controller. Explain how interrupts make the game respond quickly to the button press.
parts.answer: Pressing the button sends an interrupt signal to the processor at that moment; the processor checks for interrupts at the end of each very short cycle, so it services it almost immediately; the ISR passes the input to the game, which makes the character jump – the processor does not have to keep checking the controller and can use its time to run the game.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer is running a long calculation when two interrupts arrive at almost the same time: 'paper jam' from a printer and 'data received' from the network card, which has a higher priority. Explain how the processor deals with both interrupts and the calculation.
parts.answer: Both interrupts are placed in the interrupt queue in priority order. At the end of the current fetch-decode-execute cycle the processor finds that the network interrupt has a higher priority than the calculation, so it saves the calculation's state (register contents) and runs the network ISR. It then checks the queue again and services the paper-jam interrupt (or restores the calculation if that has higher priority). When the ISRs are finished, the saved state is restored and the calculation continues from where it stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: queue in priority order; checked at end of cycle; network handled first; state saved; ISR run; paper jam handled next/after; state restored; calculation resumes where it stopped.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the processor saves the contents of its registers before running an interrupt service routine, and what would happen if it did not.
parts.answer: The registers (e.g. program counter, accumulator) hold the current state of the task that was interrupted. The ISR uses the same registers, so it would overwrite these values. Saving them lets the processor restore them afterwards, so the original task continues from exactly where it stopped. Without saving, the task would resume at the wrong instruction or with wrong data, giving wrong results or crashing.
parts.working: 1 mark: registers hold the current task's state/PC holds next instruction; 1 mark: ISR overwrites registers; 1 mark: restored after ISR so the task resumes correctly; 1 mark: consequence of not saving.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cheap electronic toy checks its single button every few milliseconds instead of using interrupts (this is called polling). Explain why polling is acceptable for the toy, and why interrupts are essential for a laptop.
parts.answer: The toy has only one input and one simple task, so checking it constantly wastes little and the toy has nothing else to do. A laptop has many devices (keyboard, mouse, network, disk, printer) and runs many programs; checking each device constantly would waste processor time, and urgent events could be missed or delayed. Interrupts let devices signal only when they need attention, so the processor can do useful work in between and respond to the most urgent first.
parts.working: 1 mark: toy – few devices/single task so polling cost is small; 1 mark: laptop – many devices; 1 mark: polling wastes processor time; 1 mark: interrupts give a quick response with priorities.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zainab is watching a video on her smartphone when a phone call arrives. Describe how interrupts allow the phone to deal with the call and then return to the video.
parts.answer: The phone's modem/network hardware sends a high-priority interrupt when the call arrives. At the end of the current cycle the processor checks the queue, saves the state of the video app and runs the ISR. The OS pauses the video and displays the incoming-call screen and plays the ringtone. When Zainab touches the screen to answer or reject, further (touch) interrupts are generated and handled. When the call ends, the saved state is restored and the video continues from the same point.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: interrupt from the call hardware; high priority; state of video app saved; ISR/OS shows call screen; video paused; touch screen creates further interrupts; state restored and video resumes at the same point.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: While a high-priority interrupt service routine is running, a new interrupt of lower priority arrives. Explain what happens to the new interrupt.
parts.answer: It is placed in the interrupt queue and waits; the current ISR is not interrupted. It is serviced once the higher-priority work has finished (if nothing more urgent is waiting).
parts.working: 1 mark: queued/waits; 1 mark: serviced after the current higher-priority ISR completes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what could happen instead if the new interrupt had a HIGHER priority than the ISR that is running.
parts.answer: The running ISR could itself be interrupted: its state is saved, the more urgent ISR is run, and then the first ISR is restored and finished.
parts.working: 1 mark: current ISR suspended and state saved; 1 mark: higher-priority ISR runs first, then the first ISR is resumed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sensor network uses ODD parity. The parity bit is added as the left-most bit. Write the complete 8-bit byte for each 7-bit data item.
(i) 0110111
(ii) 1000010
(iii) 0001001
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) five 1s, already odd, so the parity bit is 0 (total 5); (ii) two 1s, so the parity bit is 1 (total 3); (iii) two 1s, so the parity bit is 1 (total 3).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The byte 10110100 is sent using even parity and also included in a checksum calculation. It is received as 10111110. Explain why the parity check does not detect this error.
parts.answer: Two bits have changed (both 0 → 1), so the received byte has six 1s – still an even number – and passes the even parity check.
parts.working: 1 mark: two bits changed; 1 mark: number of 1s is still even so parity is unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert both bytes to denary and explain how a checksum could detect this error.
parts.answer: Sent 180, received 190. The receiver recalculates the checksum from the data it received; because the value has increased by 10 the result will not match the checksum sent with the data, so an error is reported and the data is re-sent.
parts.working: 1 mark: 180 and 190; 1 mark: receiver recalculates the checksum using the same algorithm; 1 mark: mismatch → error detected/request resend.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Error detection (parity, checksum, echo check, check digit, ARQ)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A data logger sends five packets numbered 1 to 5 to a server using an automatic repeat request (ARQ) with positive acknowledgements and a timeout. Packet 3 arrives corrupted. The acknowledgement for packet 4 is lost on the way back.
Explain what happens to packet 3 and to packet 4.
parts.answer: Packet 3: the server's error check (e.g. checksum) fails, so it does not send a positive acknowledgement (or sends a negative one); the logger's timeout for packet 3 expires and it re-sends packet 3 automatically. Packet 4: it arrived correctly, but the logger never receives its acknowledgement, so after the timeout it re-sends packet 4 even though the server already has it.
parts.working: 1 mark: packet 3 error detected at receiver; 1 mark: no acknowledgement → timeout → re-sent; 1 mark: packet 4 acknowledgement lost → timeout expires; 1 mark: packet 4 re-sent although received correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the server must be able to recognise a duplicate packet, and how it can do so.
parts.answer: Otherwise packet 4's data would be stored twice, corrupting the file. Each packet carries a sequence number, so the server can see it already has packet 4 and discard the copy (sending another acknowledgement).
parts.working: 1 mark: duplicate would be stored twice/corrupt data; 1 mark: uses sequence numbers to identify and discard.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transmission methods (serial/parallel, simplex/duplex, USB)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement describes serial or parallel transmission.
(i) Bits are sent one after another along a single wire
(ii) Several bits are sent at the same time along separate wires
(iii) Bits can arrive out of step (skew) over long distances
(iv) Used by USB
parts.answer: (i) Serial (ii) Parallel (iii) Parallel (iv) Serial
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transmission methods (serial/parallel, simplex/duplex, USB)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define simplex data transmission.
parts.answer: Data is sent in one direction only.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A rain gauge sends readings to a data logger and never receives data. Explain why simplex is suitable, and give one other example of simplex transmission.
parts.answer: The gauge only needs to send data and the logger never needs to reply, so one direction is enough (cheaper/simpler). Other example: a computer sending data to a basic printer, or a TV broadcast/radio station to receivers.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: valid example.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transmission methods (serial/parallel, simplex/duplex, USB)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school is connecting a computer to equipment 30 m away. Explain two reasons why a serial cable is more suitable than a parallel cable.
parts.answer: 1. A parallel cable has many wires, so signals on neighbouring wires can interfere with each other (crosstalk), and bits sent together can arrive at slightly different times (skew), causing errors over 30 m; serial uses one data wire so this does not happen. 2. A serial cable has fewer wires, so it is cheaper and lighter to buy and install over a long distance.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason: identification + explanation. Accept: skew/crosstalk/interference, and cost/fewer wires.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transmission methods (serial/parallel, simplex/duplex, USB)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A link sends one bit per wire every microsecond (1 000 000 bits per second per wire). A file of 4000 bytes is sent. Ignore any extra control bits.
Calculate the time to send the file using
(i) serial transmission on one wire
(ii) parallel transmission on 8 wires, one byte at a time.
Give your answers in seconds.
parts.working: (i) 4000 × 8 = 32 000 bits ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.032 s (M1 bits, A1). (ii) 4000 bytes, one per microsecond = 0.004 s (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Despite the result, serial transmission is used for long-distance links. Explain why the parallel link would not keep its speed advantage over a long cable.
parts.answer: Over long distances the bits on the different wires arrive at slightly different times (skew) and interfere (crosstalk); to avoid errors the data rate must be slowed down or data re-sent, so the speed advantage is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: skew/crosstalk over distance; 1 mark: errors force lower rate/retransmission.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: A simple cipher replaces each letter by the letter 3 places later in the alphabet (A → D, B → E, …, X → A, Y → B, Z → C). Encrypt the plaintext LAHORE.
parts.answer: ODKRUH
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for 4 or 5 letters correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this cipher is an example of symmetric or asymmetric encryption, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Symmetric – the same key (shift by 3) is used to encrypt and to decrypt (by shifting back 3).
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric; 1 mark: same key for both.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha wants to receive confidential files from her clients using asymmetric encryption. State which key the clients use to encrypt the files and which key Ayesha uses to decrypt them.
parts.answer: Encrypt: Ayesha's public key. Decrypt: Ayesha's private key.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of Ayesha's keys can be shared with anyone.
parts.answer: Her public key.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school and an exam board share a symmetric key to protect results files. Explain why the key must be kept secret.
parts.answer: The same key decrypts the files, so anyone who obtains it can decrypt (read) and could change the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: same key encrypts and decrypts; 1 mark: anyone with it can read the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the key could be shared safely.
parts.answer: Send it using asymmetric encryption, or deliver it in person/by a separate secure channel.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement applies to symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption or both.
(i) Uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt
(ii) Uses a public key and a private key
(iii) Turns plaintext into ciphertext
(iv) The decryption key never has to be sent to the sender
parts.answer: (i) Symmetric (ii) Asymmetric (iii) Both (iv) Asymmetric
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: A message was encrypted by shifting each letter 4 places forward in the alphabet (A → E, …, W → A, X → B, Y → C, Z → D). The ciphertext is XEBMPE. Decrypt it.
parts.answer: TAXILA
parts.working: 2 marks; 1 mark for 4 or 5 letters correct. Shift each letter back 4 places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this type of cipher is not secure.
parts.answer: There are only 25 possible shifts, so an attacker can try every key quickly (brute force); letter frequencies also stay the same, so common letters can be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark: very few possible keys; 1 mark: all can be tried quickly/frequency analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: A symmetric key that is 8 bits long has 2⁸ = 256 possible values. Calculate the number of possible keys for a 16-bit key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why keys used in practice are 128 bits or longer.
parts.answer: Each extra bit doubles the number of possible keys; with 2¹²⁸ keys (about 3.4 × 10³⁸) a brute-force attack trying every key would take far too long, even with very fast computers.
parts.working: 1 mark: more bits → many more possible keys (doubles per bit); 1 mark: brute-force attack becomes impractical.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how asymmetric encryption solves the problem of sharing a secret key that occurs with symmetric encryption.
parts.answer: In symmetric encryption the secret key must be sent to the receiver and could be intercepted. With asymmetric encryption the receiver publishes a public key, which is only used to encrypt; the private key that decrypts never leaves the receiver, so nothing secret has to be sent.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric key must be transmitted and could be intercepted; 1 mark: public key can be shared openly/only encrypts; 1 mark: private key kept by owner and never transmitted.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends, Ali and Sana, use a messaging app that uses asymmetric encryption. Describe how the keys are used when Ali sends a message to Sana and when Sana replies.
parts.answer: Each person has their own key pair. Ali encrypts his message with Sana's public key; only Sana's private key can decrypt it. For the reply, Sana encrypts with Ali's public key and Ali decrypts with his own private key.
parts.working: 1 mark: each user has a public and private key pair; 1 mark: Ali uses Sana's public key; 1 mark: Sana decrypts with her private key; 1 mark: reverse for the reply (Ali's public key / Ali's private key).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An attacker's computer can test 1 000 000 000 (10⁹) keys every second. Calculate the longest time it would take to try every key for
(i) a 40-bit key, in minutes
(ii) a 56-bit key, in days.
Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: (i) 18.3 minutes (ii) 834 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results show about choosing key length.
parts.answer: Adding 16 bits multiplies the time by 2¹⁶ (65 536), so longer keys make brute-force attacks impractical.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Asymmetric encryption is slower than symmetric encryption. Many systems therefore use asymmetric encryption only to send a symmetric key, and then use that symmetric key to encrypt the rest of the data. Explain why this combination is used.
parts.answer: Symmetric encryption is fast, so it is good for large amounts of data, but its key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption solves the sharing problem because the symmetric key can be encrypted with the receiver's public key and only decrypted with their private key. Using asymmetric for the small key and symmetric for the bulk data gives both security and speed.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric is faster/suitable for large data; 1 mark: symmetric key-distribution problem; 1 mark: key sent encrypted with receiver's public key; 1 mark: combination gives secure key exchange and fast bulk encryption.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Hira sends contracts to Bilal encrypted with Bilal's public key. A hacker steals Bilal's private key.
Explain the effect of this on (i) contracts that the hacker has already intercepted and (ii) messages that Bilal sends to Hira encrypted with Hira's public key.
parts.answer: (i) The hacker can now decrypt every contract encrypted with Bilal's public key, including ones intercepted earlier – their confidentiality is lost. (ii) These are not affected: they can only be decrypted with Hira's private key, which has not been stolen.
parts.working: 2 marks for (i): can decrypt; includes earlier intercepted messages. 2 marks for (ii): still secure; needs Hira's private key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what Bilal should do now.
parts.answer: Generate a new key pair, stop using (revoke) the old public key and give Hira the new public key.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the packet number (sequence number) in a packet header.
parts.answer: So the packets can be put back into the correct order at the destination.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the destination IP address in the header.
parts.answer: So routers know where to send the packet.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name given to the part of a packet that holds the actual data being sent.
parts.answer: The payload.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of a router in packet switching.
parts.answer: It reads the destination IP address in each packet's header and decides the best next route/hop, forwarding the packet towards its destination.
parts.working: 1 mark: reads destination address in header; 1 mark: chooses route/forwards to next router.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by packet switching.
parts.answer: Data is broken into packets; each packet is sent independently and may take a different route to the destination, where they are reassembled.
parts.working: 1 mark: data split into packets sent separately; 1 mark: each can take a different route and they are reordered at the destination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one item, other than the packet number and IP addresses, that is in a packet header.
parts.answer: The size of the packet (or the total number of packets in the message).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image of 52 000 bytes is sent over a network. Each packet can carry a payload of up to 1400 bytes. Calculate the number of packets needed.
parts.answer: 38 packets
parts.working: 52 000 ÷ 1400 = 37.14… (M1); a part-packet still needs a whole packet, so 38 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the size of the payload in the last packet.
parts.answer: 200 bytes

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the packets of one email may arrive at the destination in a different order from the order in which they were sent.
parts.answer: Each packet is routed separately; routers choose the best route at that moment, so packets may take different routes; some routes are longer or more congested, so later packets can arrive before earlier ones.
parts.working: 1 mark each: packets routed independently; different routes chosen (based on traffic/availability); routes have different delays.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: A file is sent as 20 packets, but packet 13 never arrives. Explain how the receiving computer knows that a packet is missing and what happens next.
parts.answer: The header shows the total number of packets and each packet's number, so after a time the receiver sees that packet 13 has not arrived. It requests that packet again (or the sender times out with no acknowledgement and re-sends it). The file is reassembled once packet 13 arrives.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses packet numbers/total count to detect the gap; 1 mark: request re-send/timeout; 1 mark: reassembled when complete.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: A packet header contains both the sender's IP address and the destination IP address. Explain why each is needed.
parts.answer: Destination address: so routers can forward the packet to the correct device. Sender address: so the receiver knows where it came from and can send replies, acknowledgements or requests for a missing packet back to the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The trailer contains an error-checking value. Describe how it is used by the receiver.
parts.answer: The receiver recalculates the value (e.g. checksum) from the payload it received and compares it with the value in the trailer; if they differ the packet is corrupted and is requested again.
parts.working: 1 mark: recalculate and compare; 1 mark: mismatch → error → re-send.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A video clip of 3 000 000 bytes is sent in packets that each carry a payload of exactly 1500 bytes. Each packet also has a header and trailer that together add 64 bytes.
Calculate the total number of bytes transmitted.
parts.answer: 3 128 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the transmitted bytes that are header and trailer. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Multan holds a video consultation with a specialist in London. Compare sending the video by packet switching with sending it along one fixed, dedicated route reserved for the whole call. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of packet switching.
parts.answer: Advantages: packets can be re-routed around a broken or busy link, so the call can continue; no line needs to be reserved, so the network is shared efficiently and is cheaper; only lost packets need re-sending. Disadvantage: packets may arrive out of order or be delayed by different amounts, so the video may freeze or stutter (jitter/latency) while packets are reordered.
parts.working: 2 marks per advantage (point + explanation, max 4); 1 mark for a valid disadvantage linked to video.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A network has routers P, Q, R, S, T and U. The links are: P–Q, P–R, Q–S, R–S, R–T, S–U and T–U. A message is sent from a computer at P to a computer at U.
Give two different routes the packets could take.
parts.answer: e.g. P–Q–S–U and P–R–T–U (also P–R–S–U)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid routes using only listed links.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The link S–U becomes very busy. Explain how packet switching allows the message to arrive without delay.
parts.answer: Routers choose the route for each packet at the time it is sent, so packets reaching R are sent via T to U, avoiding S–U; packets are not forced to wait for the busy link.
parts.working: 1 mark: route chosen per packet/dynamically; 1 mark: P–R–T–U avoids the busy link.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the packets still need to be reassembled at U.
parts.answer: Packets on different routes may arrive in a different order, so they are reordered using the packet numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: A live cricket match is streamed over the internet. Explain why delays in some packets cause problems for live streaming, but not for downloading a file.
parts.answer: Live video must be played in order, as it arrives; if packets are late or missing the player must wait (buffering) or skip, so the picture freezes. A downloaded file is only used when all packets have arrived and been reordered, so delays only make the download take slightly longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: live stream needs packets in time and in order; 1 mark: late/lost packets cause freezing/buffering/lower quality; 1 mark: file download can wait for all packets before use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way a streaming service reduces this problem.
parts.answer: It buffers a few seconds of video before playing (or reduces video quality/resolution when the connection is slow).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Packets and packet switching

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the packets of a web page from when they leave the web server until the page appears on the user's screen. Refer to the header, routers and the destination computer.
parts.answer: The web page data is split into packets; each gets a header (sender and destination IP, packet number, total packets/size) and a trailer (error check). Each packet travels independently; routers read the destination IP and forward each packet along the best available route. At the destination, the trailer value is checked for errors and corrupted or missing packets are requested again. Packets are reordered using their packet numbers and reassembled into the web page, which the browser then displays.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: data split into packets; header contents; routers read destination IP and forward; packets may take different routes; error check using trailer; missing/corrupt packets re-sent; reordered by packet number and reassembled.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by robotics.
parts.answer: The branch of computer science (and engineering) that deals with the design, construction and operation of robots.
parts.working: 1 mark: area of computer science/engineering; 1 mark: design, construction and operation of robots.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two different ways robots are used in agriculture.
parts.answer: e.g. harvesting/picking crops; weeding (identifying and removing weeds); drones spraying crops or monitoring crop health; milking cows; planting seeds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A robot arm in a bottling factory picks up bottles and places them in crates. State the purpose of each part of the robot.
(i) The sensors
(ii) The microprocessor
(iii) The end effector (gripper)
parts.answer: (i) Detect data about the surroundings, e.g. whether a bottle is in position. (ii) Processes the sensor data and makes decisions/controls the actuators using the stored program. (iii) The tool at the end of the arm that grips and releases the bottle.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online shop's warehouse in Karachi uses robots to move shelves to packing stations. Give two advantages to the company of using these robots.
parts.answer: e.g. they can work 24 hours a day without breaks; they are faster and more consistent than people; fewer picking errors; lower wage costs over time; can work in cold/hazardous areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage to the company.
parts.answer: e.g. high cost to buy, set up and maintain; need specialist staff to program/repair them; if they break down, work stops.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two different uses of robots in medicine.
parts.answer: e.g. assisting surgeons with precise operations; dispensing medicines in a pharmacy; disinfecting hospital rooms with UV light; delivering supplies around a hospital; robotic prosthetic limbs; rehabilitation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A robot vacuum cleaner moves around a flat on its own. Explain how it uses sensors, a microprocessor and actuators to avoid bumping into furniture and to avoid falling down stairs.
parts.answer: Infrared/ultrasonic (proximity) sensors detect objects ahead; downward-facing sensors detect a drop such as a stair edge. The data is converted to digital and sent to the microprocessor, which compares it with stored values. If an object is too close or a drop is detected, the microprocessor sends signals to the actuators (wheel motors) to stop, reverse or turn. This is repeated continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable sensors for obstacles and drops; 1 mark: microprocessor compares readings with stored values; 1 mark: actuators/motors told to stop/turn; 1 mark: continuous loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the robot knows when to return to its charging base.
parts.answer: The microprocessor monitors the battery level; when it falls below a stored value it directs the robot back to the base (using its map or a signal from the base).
parts.working: 1 mark: battery level monitored and compared with a threshold; 1 mark: navigates back to the base.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Drones are used to deliver medicines to remote villages in mountain areas. Explain how a delivery drone shows the three characteristics of a robot.
parts.answer: Mechanical structure: it has a frame, propellers and a parcel holder. Electrical components: it has sensors (GPS, cameras, altitude sensors), a microprocessor and motors (actuators). Programmable: it is programmed with its route and delivery instructions, which can be changed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mechanical structure/framework; electrical components – sensors, microprocessor, actuators; programmable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using drones for these deliveries.
parts.answer: Advantage: faster than road travel on mountain roads/reaches places that are hard to get to. Disadvantage: limited load and battery range/cannot fly in bad weather/may be damaged or lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: The police use a remotely controlled robot to inspect a suspicious package. Explain two reasons for using a robot rather than a person.
parts.answer: 1. Safety: if the package explodes the robot is damaged instead of a person being injured or killed. 2. The robot's cameras and sensors can examine the package closely and send images to officers at a safe distance; it can use tools steadily and precisely, without nerves.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason (reason + explanation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this robot is still operated by a human rather than acting by itself.
parts.answer: Each situation is different and needs human judgement; a mistake would be very dangerous, so a trained person decides each action.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two uses of robots in entertainment.
parts.answer: e.g. animatronic characters in theme parks that move and speak; camera robots that move smoothly to film sports or movies; robot toys and pets; drones performing light shows.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two described uses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using a robot camera arm to film a cricket match.
parts.answer: It can repeat the same precise, smooth movement at high speed every time, giving consistent shots that a human camera operator could not hold steadily.
parts.working: 1 mark: precision/repeatability/speed; 1 mark: linked explanation.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chain of restaurants in Karachi is planning to use robots to carry food from the kitchen to customers' tables. Evaluate this plan, considering the restaurant owner, the staff and the customers.
parts.answer: Owner: high initial cost and maintenance, but lower wage costs, works long hours without breaks, consistent service; novelty may attract customers. Staff: some waiters may lose jobs or have fewer hours; others may need retraining to supervise and maintain robots; heavy carrying reduced. Customers: novelty/consistent delivery, but less personal service; robots cannot answer complex questions or deal with problems; possible spills if they collide. Conclusion: likely to work best with robots helping, not fully replacing, staff.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per stakeholder for balanced points (advantages and disadvantages); for 6 marks there must be a reasoned conclusion. Max 4 if only advantages or only disadvantages are given.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory robot that paints car doors can be reprogrammed to paint a new model. Explain how the robot can be programmed, and why this makes it more useful than a fixed machine built for one task.
parts.answer: It can be programmed by writing a program of movements, or by an operator guiding the arm through the painting movements once so that it records and then repeats them. Because it is programmable, the same robot can be given new instructions when the factory changes models, so no new machine is needed – saving cost and time.
parts.working: 1 mark: programmed with a sequence of instructions; 1 mark: e.g. by being guided through movements which are stored/recorded; 1 mark: can be reprogrammed for new tasks; 1 mark: saves cost/time compared with replacing a fixed machine.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A courier company uses a robot arm with a camera to sort parcels by size onto three conveyor belts. Describe how the robot works, from the camera capturing an image to the parcel being placed on the correct belt.
parts.answer: A parcel arrives and a sensor detects it; the camera captures an image. The microprocessor processes the image to measure the parcel's size and compares it with stored size limits. It decides which belt is needed and sends signals to the actuators (motors in the arm). The end effector (e.g. a suction gripper) picks up the parcel, the arm moves to the correct belt and releases it. The process repeats for the next parcel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: sensor detects parcel; camera image captured; microprocessor calculates size; compares with stored values; signals sent to actuators; gripper picks up and places on correct belt; repeated continuously.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how artificial intelligence could improve the robot over time.
parts.answer: With machine learning it could learn from previous mistakes/more examples to recognise unusual shapes and sort them more accurately.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Robotics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory in Sialkot plans to let robot arms and human workers work side by side on the same production line. Explain three measures that should be taken to keep the workers safe.
parts.answer: 1. Proximity/pressure sensors on the robot detect a person nearby and the microprocessor slows or stops the arm. 2. Emergency stop buttons within reach of every worker cut power to the robots instantly. 3. Limiting force and speed, or marked safety zones/light curtains, so the robot stops if someone enters its area. (Also: training for workers; regular maintenance and testing of safety systems.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each measure: 1 for the measure, 1 for how it protects workers.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an automated system.
parts.answer: A combination of software and hardware (sensors, microprocessor, actuators) designed to carry out a task automatically, without human intervention.
parts.working: 1 mark: hardware and software working together; 1 mark: performs tasks without human involvement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: A juice factory in Multan is automated. Give two advantages and two disadvantages of using automated systems in the factory.
parts.answer: Advantages: faster production; works 24/7 without breaks; consistent quality/fewer errors; safer for workers in dangerous tasks; lower running costs. Disadvantages: expensive to set up; expensive to maintain/needs skilled technicians; may break down and stop production; loss of jobs; less flexible when something unexpected happens.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name a suitable sensor for each automated system.
(i) Street lights that switch on at dusk
(ii) A shop door that opens when a customer approaches
(iii) Reversing sensors on a car that warn of obstacles
(iv) A fire-alarm system in a hotel
parts.answer: (i) Light sensor (ii) Infrared/motion sensor (iii) Proximity (ultrasonic) sensor (iv) Smoke/gas sensor (accept temperature sensor)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: An automatic car wash detects a car with sensors and then washes it. Give two actuators the car wash would use and state what each does.
parts.answer: e.g. motors that turn the brushes; pumps that spray water/soap; valves that open water flow; motors that move the gantry or conveyor; fans/heaters for drying.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two actuators with their function.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many sensors in automated systems produce analogue signals. State why an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is needed.
parts.answer: The microprocessor can only process digital (binary) data, so the analogue signal from the sensor must be converted to digital before it can be processed.
parts.working: 1 mark: sensor output is analogue; 1 mark: microprocessor needs digital data.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an automated street-lighting system switches the lights on in the evening and off in the morning.
parts.answer: A light sensor measures the light level continuously. The reading is converted from analogue to digital by an ADC and sent to the microprocessor. The microprocessor compares it with a stored value. If the light level is below the stored value and the lights are off, it sends a signal to switch them on; if it is above the value and the lights are on, it switches them off. This is repeated continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each: light sensor; ADC; compared with stored value; signal to actuator/switch on or off; continuous loop.

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: A driverless metro train stops automatically at each station. Explain how the automated system makes the train stop in the correct place at the platform.
parts.answer: Sensors (e.g. position markers on the track, speed sensors) send data to the train's microprocessor. The microprocessor compares the train's position and speed with stored values for the station stopping point. It sends signals to the actuators to reduce power and apply the brakes gradually. When the train is stopped at the correct position, it opens the doors (platform screen doors also open).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: sensors detect position/speed; data sent to microprocessor; compared with stored stopping point/speed profile; brakes/motors controlled by actuators; doors opened only when stopped correctly; continuous monitoring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage to passengers of the trains being automated.
parts.answer: More frequent and reliable service/precise timing; smoother braking; stops exactly at the platform doors.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A poultry farm in Punjab uses an automated system to keep the chicken shed between 21 °C and 25 °C. It has a temperature sensor, a heater and fans. Describe how the system keeps the temperature in this range.
parts.answer: The temperature sensor sends readings, via an ADC, to the microprocessor. The microprocessor compares each reading with the stored values 21 and 25. If the temperature is below 21 °C it switches the heater on (and fans off). If it is above 25 °C it switches the fans on and the heater off. If it is in range, both can be off. The process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sensor reading via ADC to microprocessor; compared with stored values; below 21 → heater on; above 25 → fans on/heater off; continuous loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A virtual-reality game uses a headset that contains motion sensors (accelerometers and gyroscopes). Explain how the game automatically updates what the player sees.
parts.answer: The sensors detect the movement and rotation of the player's head; the data is sent to the processor, which calculates the new direction of view; the game redraws the scene for that direction many times a second so the view changes with the player's movement.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sensors detect movement/rotation; processor calculates new viewpoint; display updated continuously (in real time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other way automated systems are used in gaming.
parts.answer: e.g. haptic feedback controllers that vibrate automatically; cameras that track body movement; game AI controlling opponents; automatic adjustment of difficulty.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An automated bottling line fills bottles of mineral water. Explain how the system makes sure that under-filled bottles do not reach customers.
parts.answer: A sensor (e.g. light/infrared sensor or weight sensor) checks the fill level of every bottle as it passes. The microprocessor compares the reading with the stored acceptable level. If the bottle is under-filled, the microprocessor sends a signal to an actuator (e.g. a pusher arm) that removes it from the conveyor. Correctly filled bottles continue to be capped and packed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sensor checks each bottle; compared with stored value; actuator rejects under-filled bottle; continuous for every bottle/others continue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An automated flood-warning system monitors the water level of a river near a village. Describe how the system could warn the villagers.
parts.answer: A water-level sensor continuously measures the river level; readings are sent to a microprocessor/computer, which compares them with stored danger levels. If the level is above a threshold, it automatically sets off sirens/flashing lights and sends text messages to villagers and the local authority. Readings are also stored so the rate of rise can be monitored.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: level sensor; continuous readings; compared with threshold; automatic alarm/siren; SMS/alerts sent; data logged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why automation is more suitable than a person checking the river.
parts.answer: It monitors 24 hours a day including at night and in storms, and reacts immediately; a person could not watch continuously and would be in danger near a flooding river.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A busy junction in Rawalpindi has automated traffic lights that change their timings depending on the traffic. Describe how sensors, a microprocessor and actuators are used, and how the timing changes when a long queue builds up on one road.
parts.answer: Sensors (induction loops in the road, or cameras/infrared sensors) count vehicles and detect queues on each approach. The data is sent to the microprocessor, which compares queue lengths and waiting times with stored values. It sends signals to the actuators that switch the light bulbs/LEDs. If one road has a long queue, the microprocessor lengthens the green time for that road and shortens it for quieter roads, while keeping a minimum and maximum time so no road waits too long. Pedestrian buttons are also inputs. The process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: suitable sensors; counts/queue data sent to microprocessor; compared with stored values; actuators change lights; green time increased for the busy road; limits on min/max time; pedestrian requests; continuous loop.

subtopic: Automated systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemical plant uses an automated system to control the temperature and pressure in its reaction vessels. Evaluate relying on the automated system for safety, and explain why a manual override is still needed.
parts.answer: Benefits: monitors continuously and reacts faster than a person; can shut valves or start cooling instantly; works in dangerous areas without putting people at risk; consistent and does not get tired. Drawbacks: sensors can fail or give false readings; software errors or power failure could stop it working; it may not cope with situations it was not programmed for; vulnerable to cyber attacks. Manual override lets trained operators take control in an emergency or when the system is faulty, so a fault does not lead to an explosion or leak.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for benefits and drawbacks (must include both); up to 2 marks for reasons for a manual override; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An automated air-conditioning system in an office turns the cooling on when the temperature is above 26 °C and off when it is below 22 °C. Between 22 °C and 26 °C it leaves the cooling as it is. Write an algorithm, in pseudocode, for the microprocessor. Assume ReadTemp() returns the current temperature and CoolingOn() and CoolingOff() control the actuator.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Temp : REAL
WHILE TRUE
   Temp ← ReadTemp()
   IF Temp > 26 THEN
      CALL CoolingOn()
   ELSE
      IF Temp < 22 THEN
         CALL CoolingOff()
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark: infinite/continuous loop; 1 mark: temperature read inside the loop; 1 mark: > 26 turns cooling on; 1 mark: < 22 turns cooling off; 1 mark: no action between 22 and 26 (no ELSE that changes the state).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the system uses two different temperatures instead of one.
parts.answer: To stop the cooling switching on and off very frequently around one value, which wastes energy and wears out the equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car has adaptive cruise control, which keeps a safe distance behind the vehicle in front. The system uses a 2-second rule: the safe distance is the distance the car travels in 2 seconds. Calculate the safe distance, in metres, when the car is travelling at 90 km/h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the adaptive cruise control system keeps this distance.
parts.answer: A radar/ultrasonic sensor at the front measures the distance to the vehicle ahead and sends it to the microprocessor, which also knows the car's speed. The microprocessor calculates the safe distance and compares it with the measured distance. If the gap is too small it sends signals to actuators to reduce the throttle or apply the brakes; if the gap is larger and the car is below the set speed it accelerates. This is repeated continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sensor measures distance; microprocessor compares with calculated safe distance; actuators brake/slow or accelerate; continuous loop.

parts.text:
An office has 40 lights, each using 20 W. Without automation, the lights are on for 12 hours a day. An automated system with motion and light sensors reduces this to 8 hours a day.
Calculate the energy saved in 30 days, in kWh, and the money saved if electricity costs Rs 50 per kWh.
parts.answer: 96 kWh; Rs 4800

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the motion and light sensors are used together to decide when to switch the lights on.
parts.answer: The lights are switched on only when the motion sensor detects someone in the room AND the light sensor shows natural light is below a stored level; otherwise they are switched off.
parts.working: 1 mark: motion sensor detects people; 1 mark: light level also compared with stored value – both conditions needed.
